What's so amazing about elephants?

The largest animal on land, the elephant, is an amazing animal that grabs objects and drinks water with its long trunk. There are secrets in its big ears and tusks, too.

Curious about the story of the elephant picture book? Let's look at the lesson of the elephant picture book along with the pictures. Come meet the key scenes of the elephant picture book's story, too. Read the elephant picture book together with your child and talk about the story.

content.text:
Nature and science facts about elephants

An elephant's long trunk is an organ that combines the upper lip and the nose, and thanks to its countless muscles it grabs objects like a hand, draws up water and pours it into its mouth to drink, and even plucks high leaves to eat. Its big ears act like fans that flap to cool the heat from its body, and the hard tusks (ivory) sticking out of its mouth are not horns but teeth that have grown long.

Great points to observe together

Point out things like the long trunk (hand, water, food), the big ears (cooling off), the tusks (teeth), and herd life. It's great to talk together about, "What can you do with a trunk?"

content.text:
Parent guide — how to grow curiosity

Swing your arm like a trunk and act out "grabbing objects and drinking water." Experience the role of the big ears (cooling off) by fanning, and telling your child "the tusks are actually teeth" will make it even more interesting.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What does an elephant do with its trunk?
A. It grabs objects like a hand, draws up water to drink, and plucks high leaves to eat. It has a great many muscles.

Q. Are the tusks horns?
A. No. They are teeth (ivory) that have grown long. They are not horns.

Q. How can we observe them at home?
A. Imitating a trunk with your arm, experiencing the ears' role by fanning, and talking about "tusks = teeth" all work well.
